findings.title: Tag and remote values allow arbitrary shell execution
findings.rationale: Both caller-controlled values are interpolated into a command executed through a shell. `remote` is completely unquoted, and double quotes around the tag still permit shell expansions such as `$(...)` and backticks. A malicious value can therefore execute arbitrary commands with the release process's privileges. Replace `execSync` with `execFileSync("git", ["push", "--", remote, `refs/tags/${tag}`])` (and validate that the tag is an acceptable Git ref) so no shell parses either value.

findings.title: firstEntries returns count plus one elements
findings.rationale: The loop includes `i === count`, so `firstEntries(lines, 0)` returns one item and every positive count returns one too many. If `count` reaches or exceeds `lines.length`, it also inserts `undefined` despite the declared `string[]` return type. Use an exclusive bound (`i < count`) while also bounding to the available entries, or simply return `lines.slice(0, count)`.

findings.title: withFooter mutates the caller-owned release note
findings.rationale: Despite promising a copy, the function pushes into the original `highlights` array and returns the same note object. Callers retaining the original observe an unexpected footer, and repeated use accumulates mutations. Return a new object with a new array, for example `{ ...note, highlights: [...note.highlights, footer] }`.

findings.title: Successful Git response is discarded from the return value
findings.rationale: `execSync` returns only the child's stdout, while `git push` writes its normal remote/status response to stderr. Consequently this function commonly returns an empty string even after a successful push, contrary to its contract. Capture both streams explicitly using a spawn API, or redefine the API to return structured status rather than treating stdout as the server response.

summary: The module contains a directly exploitable shell-command injection plus deterministic boundary, mutation, and output-stream defects. No test files or runnable test configuration were present, so no tests could be observed passing; the documented behaviors are not backed by visible tests.
